As animals, we receive information every day through our senses. Within us, we have the ability to process this sensory data in order to understand the world around us. I believe that from the very beginning, we have the capacity to recognise where this information comes from. For example, if I observe a sheep, my brain is able to understand that the white colour, the shape, and the smell all come from the same object (the sheep).

We also have the ability to generalise. So, if I see another living being with the same or similar characteristics, I can relate it to the one I saw before (the sheep) and say, “That is the same type of object I have already seen.”

We are capable of understanding cause‑and‑effect relationships as well. For instance, if I see a ram charge at a wooden fence and break it, I know that the fence is broken because of the ram’s action. 

Through these observations we gain experience, which we can later use to achieve our purpose. So, if I want to break another section of fencing, I know that one possible method would be to make the ram charge at it.

The point is, why I would do that, maybe it is something necessary to archive something bigger like for example free all animals? What does mean have a goal? 

Another thing to consider is this: if we learn through experience, who teaches a duckling, the moment it hatches, to start following the first moving shape it sees? Or who teaches a baby to suckle as soon as its mouth touches the breast? Clearly, we already have something within us that allows us to take our first steps in the world.

Those are some of my starting points for thinking the software 🙂

Yes, LLMs while it can give you the probabilities for the most likely next token, doesn't include a confidence score of how likely the token is to lead to a good outcome (such as in the case of an language model, that would be a good reaction to it's output).

Some people have tried to fix this by creating Bayesian models, but I think without much success.

I think confidence levels would mostly have to be acquired in post-training reinforcement learning stage. Although to help it along in the training stage the AI should learn what sources it's information came from (journals/twitter/reddit) and also use that to adjust it's confidence levels. In a dreaming, simulation (self-play) mode, it could probably also acquire confidence predictions, as it learns which moves lead to good outcomes. (Similar to how Alpha-zero works). As it trains to increase it's confidence levels, this should be in some-way equivalent to world-building.

If we consider "confidence" and it's opposite "doubt" as emotions. Then what we are talking about is imbuing the AGI with ruidementary emotions. 

Humans tend to ruminate on things which they have low confidence on. Simulating things over and over in their mind until confidence of the corrected course of action is achieved. Not only that but in an open ended topic like mathematics there will always be places where a human is not confident and this spurs them on to new discoveries.

TLDR. Confidence is all you need.

firstMessage.rawMarkdown:
Participating in ARC-AGI-3 has been one of the more philosophically disorienting experiences I've had in AI development. Not because the benchmark is hard (it is), but because it forced me to question what I thought I understood about intelligence.

Most definitions of AGI I've encountered frame it as capability breadth: a system that can do anything a human can do. I've come to think that's the wrong frame entirely.

From where I stand - drawing on cognitive science, epistemology, and a bit of continental philosophy - AGI is not about maximal capability. It's about the capacity to recognize one's own limits, and from that recognition, find the direction to expand them.

A system that can't fail gracefully, that can't say "I don't have the right frame for this," that can't distinguish between what it knows and what it's pattern-matching toward - that system isn't intelligent. It's just fast.

---

On the IPO problem nobody talks about

I've noticed that most ARC discussions circle around Input → Process → Output. The refinement loop. The architecture. The reasoning chain.

Very rarely do I see anyone seriously address the D that has to precede the : Data.

Not training data in the conventional sense. I mean: where does the *substrate* come from? What is the node pool from which any input draws meaning? If you don't have a structured semantic foundation that a system can anchor concepts to, then your Input isn't really input - it's noise looking for a pattern to land on.

This is actually what ARC-AGI-3 is surfacing, I think. The games don't give you data. They give you *interaction*. And the gap between those two things is where most AI systems fall apart.

Humans don't struggle with LS20 because they have more compute. They don't struggle because they've seen similar games. They succeed because they arrive with a pre-structured world model - a massive, mostly-unconscious graph of named concepts, relations, and frames - and they collapse that graph onto the novel environment almost instantly.

That pre-structure is the data layer. And it's almost entirely absent in current agent architectures.

---

What I'm building alongside this contest

I have a personal AI project running in parallel - Pete - and the repo linked here is specifically the data layer: a ~100k node fractal semantic graph that functions as a cognitive substrate.

The design philosophy came from a simple observation:

In cognitive science, consciousness is often modeled as a *dynamic activation pattern* over a much larger unconscious structure. Attention doesn't create the content it attends to - it selects from what's already there.

So Pete doesn't encode information as vectors. It encodes it as named nodes organized by meaning and frame of reference. The full graph is the unconscious. Active attention is a small, focused subgraph pulled from it based on context.

Same substrate. Different attention pattern. Different frame. Different "persona."

The claim isn't that this produces consciousness. The claim is that without this kind of pre-structured semantic substrate, any input processing is fundamentally impoverished - because the system has no stable ground to anchor new concepts against.

This maps directly to what I see failing in ARC-AGI-3 agents: they process the frame they're given, but they have no deep structure to place it in. No world model to collapse onto the novel environment. No way to recognize that what looks like a rotator here is the same structural role as a switch somewhere else - because they're not tracking Meaning across Name changes.

---

A different question about AGI

I'll leave with the question that's been sitting with me throughout this contest:

If a system can't recognize that its current frame might be wrong - if it can't step back from its own processing and ask "wait, am I even using the right lens here?" - can we really call it intelligent?

Maybe the benchmark for AGI isn't solving every task. Maybe it's the capacity to know when you're at the edge of your current understanding, and do something coherent with that knowledge rather than just failing louder.

Interested to hear how others are thinking about the data substrate problem - and whether the distinction between Input and the pre-structured ground that makes Input meaningful resonates with anyone else here.

Git: https://github.com/jkdkr2439/Pete_Unconscious_Substrate
